ground: Men are qawwāmūn over women: they stand in charge of them and maintain them. This is by what God has given some of them over others, and by what they have spent from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, and they guard in absence (the husband's absence, and what is unseen) by what God has guarded. As for those whose nushūz (rising against the marriage) you fear, admonish them, leave them alone in the beds, and strike them. If they obey you, seek no way against them. God is High, Great.

triggers.how: same root by the dictionary's own analysis (B012: the particle ʿalā counted under ع ل و): men stand 'over' women
same particle: some given more 'over' others
same particle: 'seek no way over/against them'
shared scene of height: nushūz B001 is high ground, what juts up
paired closing attribute (the High, the Great, as in 22:62, 31:30, 34:23, 40:12)

findings.statement: The ayah plainly assigns men a standing responsibility and closes on God's attributes, and in the Arabic that responsibility is spoken three times with ʿalā ('over') and then answered by God's name ʿAliyy ('the One who is over', from the same letters).
findings.perceptible: The ayah becomes a vertical map. Men stand over; some are raised over others; a wife may 'rise' (nushūz); the husband is forbidden to seek a road 'over' her. The last word puts God above every height in the household. So the man's 'over' is a position of duty held under a higher One, not a summit. The Turkish reader cannot hear this chain, because 'üzerinde', 'karşı' and 'Yüce' are unrelated words in Turkish.

triggers.how: only other uses of the lemma; same surah: 'be qawwāmīn for justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves'
'be qawwāmīn for God, witnesses in justice'

findings.statement: Qawwāmūn plainly means men are responsible for and maintain women, and the lemma's only other two uses name a constant standing-up for justice and for God, even against one's own interest.
findings.perceptible: In the Quran, qawwām is always a charge laid on its bearer, never a privilege for him to enjoy. The intensive form (someone who stands repeatedly and persistently) makes the man's position a continual labour. Later in this same surah it is tied to justice even against himself (4:135). Read that way, the charge falls on the man's own conduct as much as on the household.

triggers.how: shared scene wealth.property: qiwām is 'what sustains life and livelihood'
syntax: 'by what they spent of their wealth' grounds the qawwāma
neighbouring: bonds and allotted shares

findings.statement: The qawwām is plainly one who takes charge, and the root's branches of standing upright (B002), keeping level (B008), guarding (B004) and being the qiwām, the support a thing stands on and the livelihood that keeps it alive (B009), gather into one concept: he is the pillar that keeps the household standing by supplying it.
findings.perceptible: The ayah gives two grounds. The second one ('by what they spent') is material. The man stands over the household the way a pillar stands under a roof, and the root holds both. His height exists in order to hold something up. The Turkish word 'kıvam' (consistency) keeps a faint trace of this sense of what keeps a thing standing.

triggers.how: the partner term of the comparison
same formula two ayat earlier, addressed to men and women together, followed by 'to men a share... to women a share'

findings.statement: The ayah plainly grounds the men's charge in God's giving 'some of them over others', and it does not say 'men over women': the masculine pronoun hum covers both groups, and the formula repeats 4:32, where each side has its own portion.
findings.perceptible: Which party is given more is left as 'some... others'. This keeps the ranking functional and partial. It echoes 4:32, where coveting what God gave the other side was forbidden and each side has a naṣīb. The reader can see that the grounding is a specific allotment and not a statement about worth.

triggers.how: shared root and formula
'ask God of His faḍl': surplus open to all
neighbouring: those who hide what God gave them of His faḍl

findings.statement: Faḍḍala plainly means God gave more to some, and its root's first branch is the surplus left over after need and division (B001) and the unowed gift (B003).
findings.perceptible: The 'more' behind the man's charge is heard as surplus that is meant to flow out, as in 'by what they spent', and not to be hoarded. 4:37 condemns those who hide God's faḍl. Turkish 'fazilet' (moral virtue) narrows this to moral excellence, which is exactly what the ayah does not claim.

triggers.how: syntax
neighbouring: spending for show
neighbouring: spending from what God provided

findings.statement: Anfaqū plainly means they spent on the household, and the root's base is a thing running out and leaving (B001), so the spending that grounds the charge is wealth that actually leaves the man's hand.
findings.perceptible: The verb is past and causal ('by what they have spent'). The ground is money actually spent, not money merely owned. The neighbouring ayat (4:37–39) put stingy and showy spending right after this ayah. Turkish 'nafaka' (a legal maintenance payment) and 'infak' (charity) each keep only part of this.

triggers.how: shared scene ritual.prayer / posture.upright: qāma B002 bodily standing
concordance: qānitāt among believers' qualities before God
concordance: beside muslimāt, muʾmināt, ʿābidāt

findings.statement: Qānitāt plainly names women devoted in obedience, and its branch of long standing in prayer (B002) and silence from human talk (B004) sets a second standing beside the men's: they stand over the household, she stands before God.
findings.perceptible: The ayah has two standings. The man's standing faces the household. The woman's standing faces God. Her devotion is not defined as his possession. Turkish 'kunut' (a prayer said standing) keeps the posture, and the ayah's pairing restores the whole picture.

triggers.how: concordance
concordance

findings.statement: Qānitāt is plainly 'devoutly obedient', and in all its Quranic uses (3 of 3 for this form; the root's 13 uses) qunūt is devotion toward God, which the dictionary also extends to a wife's obedience (B001).
findings.perceptible: A translation that renders it 'obedient to their husbands' narrows a word whose Quranic address is God. The husband is not named at this point in the ayah. Only the absence (ghayb) points toward him.

triggers.how: syntax: guarders of the ghayb
same root: God guards
plan image I3: the fortress of married women

findings.statement: The wives plainly keep what should be kept while the husband is away (ghayb B005), and this is the inside of the fortress drawn in 4:24: the wife keeps its interior, and God is the guard around it.
findings.perceptible: The absence is spatial. The husband is outside the walls, and someone keeps the inside. The phrase 'by what God guarded' places God's guarding around hers, so she is not the last line of defence.

triggers.how: concordance: belief in the unseen
next ayah: God knows the inside of the matter

findings.statement: Ghayb here plainly marks the circumstance of absence, and the word's dominant Quranic role (32 of 49: the unseen that God knows) stays audible, so her guarding is done where only God sees.
findings.perceptible: Her fidelity takes place out of the husband's sight. That makes it a matter between her and God, not something under the husband's surveillance. Turkish 'gayb' hears only the mystical unseen, and 'gaip' hears only a missing person. The Arabic holds both.

triggers.how: shared root in the same clause
concordance: women and men who guard their private parts

findings.statement: Ḥāfiẓāt plainly means women who guard, and the root joins watching over (B001), keeping in memory (B002), persevering (B003), vigilance (B004) and guarding what is sacred and the pledge (B006) into one concept: steady, wakeful keeping.
findings.perceptible: The wife's guarding is active and continuous. She keeps honour, trust, the household, and the pledge in memory. The same verb is used for God, so her keeping mirrors His. Turkish 'hafız/hafıza' has narrowed this to memorisation.

triggers.how: case of the following noun changes who guards whom

findings.statement: The received reading 'by what God has guarded' makes God the guarder, and the accusative reading allāha ('by their guarding of God') makes the women keep God's due, so the two readings together describe a keeping that runs both ways.
findings.perceptible: Read together, God guards those who guard, and they guard in absence because they keep God. The keeping has two directions.

triggers.how: shared root, next ayah: 'if the two want repair'
same surah, the mirror case of the husband's nushūz: ṣulḥ is best

findings.statement: Ṣāliḥāt plainly means righteous women, and the root's branch of ending estrangement (B002) and of fitting (B003) comes back in the next ayah as iṣlāḥ between the couple.
findings.perceptible: The word that names the good wife is the same root as the repair the whole passage aims at. The ṣāliḥa is someone in whom things fit, and when fitting fails the remedy has her name. Turkish 'salih' has become 'pious' and lost the sense of reconciliation, which 'sulh' still keeps.

triggers.how: syntax
shared scene of height
plan I8: the split that follows the rising

findings.statement: Nushūz plainly is a wife's estrangement from the marriage, and its root image is ground rising and jutting up (B001), getting up from one's place (B002), and in the classical entry a mount on which saddle and rider cannot settle.
findings.perceptible: The breakdown gets a shape. Something that lay level rises up, and the shared place stops being a place where anyone can settle. The ayah answers that rising with steps and ends by naming the only One who is truly high. Turkish 'nüşuz' is a narrow legal term and has lost the ground and the body.

triggers.how: only other use of the lemma, same surah: a woman fears nushūz from her husband

findings.statement: Nushūz here is plainly the wife's, and the same word in 4:128 is the husband's, and the dictionary defines the husband's nushūz as his harshness, including striking her (نشز بعلها عليها إذا ضربها وجفاها).
findings.perceptible: The surah does not make rising up a female trait. The same word turns around in 4:128, and there the remedy is ṣulḥ. The lexicon names a husband's unwarranted blows as his own nushūz. So the third step of this ayah has a limit built into its vocabulary: once it goes beyond remedy it becomes the very rising it was meant to answer, and 'seek no way against them' draws that line.

triggers.how: parallel frame in the next ayah
same frame for the wife fearing the husband's nushūz

findings.statement: The steps are plainly triggered when a husband fears nushūz, and khawf is defined as 'expecting harm from a sign' (توقع المكروه عن أمارة), so the whole sequence hangs on evidence that is actually visible.
findings.perceptible: All three steps depend on this one conditional verb. The same fear-frame opens the arbitration in 4:35 and the wife's case in 4:128. This passage of law is written around anticipating a breakdown and repairing it, not around punishing one.

triggers.how: same surah: 'how excellent is what God admonishes you with'
concordance: Luqman to his son
concordance: God forbids baghy and admonishes

findings.statement: 'Admonish them' is plainly the first step, and waʿẓ is a reminder of consequences 'at which the heart softens' (B001), which in most Quranic uses God or a prophet or a father gives.
findings.perceptible: The first remedy borrows the register in which God speaks to people: reminding, not commanding. The aim is a softened heart. Turkish 'vaaz' (a sermon from the pulpit) makes it sound formal and public, but here it is private speech.

triggers.how: syntax: hajr located 'in' the beds
locative preposition

findings.statement: 'Leave them in the beds' plainly means withdrawing within the shared bed, and the preposition fī keeps the separation inside the place of closeness rather than outside the house.
findings.perceptible: The second step is a distance measured within the bed. It is sharp but confined, and the way back stays within reach. The shared bed (B002) remains shared even while it is cold.

triggers.how: two ayat later: 'the companion at the side' (al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb); maḍjaʿ is where the side (janb) lies
concordance: sides that leave the beds to call on their Lord

findings.statement: Maḍājiʿ are plainly beds, the places where one lies on one's side (janb, B001), and two ayat later kindness is commanded toward 'the companion at the side'.
findings.perceptible: The person next to you in bed is literally the one at your side. The surah goes straight on to command iḥsān toward the companion at the side. Some exegetes include the wife in that phrase, which is outside the dictionary. The cold side in 4:34 is followed at once by a command to be good to the one lying beside you.

triggers.how: concordance: 'leave them with a graceful leaving' (hajran jamīlan)
syntax

findings.statement: Hajr is plainly leaving them alone, and the root's core is cutting contact by body, tongue or heart (B001), the same root as hijra, departure from one place to another (B002).
findings.perceptible: The second step is a small hijra made without leaving the house. It is a stepping away meant to change the situation. The Quran elsewhere pairs it with 'graceful', and nothing in the root requires contempt. Turkish 'hicran' adds the ache of separation, which is fitting here, since the withdrawal also costs the one who withdraws.

triggers.how: shared scene tool.rope / pastoral

findings.statement: Beside the plain 'leave them', the dictionary attests hijār, a rope tying a camel's foot (B007), a sense that one classical exegete is reported to have read here.
findings.perceptible: This is kept only as a record of an attested branch and a reported reading. The plain sense of withdrawal stands.

triggers.how: direct pronoun object with no preposition, the construction of the 'striking a person' group in the concordance

findings.statement: Iḍribūhunna plainly means 'strike them' (B001). The verb's other attested branches each come with their own construction: travel with fī al-arḍ, an example with mathal, restraint with ʿan or ʿalā yadihi, a barrier with bayna. None of those is present here.
findings.perceptible: This gives the reader an honest footing. The Arabic construction here is the one for striking, and the other senses of the root can only be heard as echoes. What limits the act in this ayah comes from its setting: the fear that needs a visible sign, the order admonish–withdraw–strike, the immediate stop once they obey ('seek no way against them'), the lexicon's naming of a husband's excess as his own nushūz, and the closing reminder of God's height.

triggers.how: sequence of restraining measures
same surah: 'confine them in the houses'

findings.statement: Beside the plain 'strike them', the root carries restraining a person from an undertaking (B005, 'ḍaraba ʿalā yadihi'), withholding (B004, including أضرب في بيته 'stayed in his house') and setting a barrier (B006). These are audible as the direction of the step, to stop a course already begun, but they are not its construction.
findings.perceptible: The strike is heard as a check on a course under way, not as a penalty for something finished. That fits the conditional frame ('whose nushūz you fear'). The attested restraining senses are recorded only as resonance, because their prepositions or verb forms are absent here.

triggers.how: the limit that follows

findings.statement: The plain command to strike stands, and classical exegetes and jurists reported it as bounded: not injuring, not on the face, with something as slight as a tooth-stick, and discouraged in reports from the Prophet.
findings.perceptible: This orients the reader toward how the plain sense was received and limited in the tradition. It comes from tafsir memory, not from the dictionary.

triggers.how: joined by wa
joined by wa

findings.statement: The three steps are plainly listed in order, and the conjunction wa does not by itself impose a sequence. The graded reading (one step only if the one before fails) comes from the context and from the jurists.
findings.perceptible: The reader should know that the steps rising from word to withdrawal to strike are the ayah's evident order, and that the jurists made that order binding. The ordering particle fa appears only at the start (fa-ʿiẓūhunna).

triggers.how: next ayah: God makes the two fit
opposite of rising

findings.statement: 'If they obey you' plainly means the wife returns to compliance, and ṭāʿa also names mutual accord, when one side goes along with the other (muṭāwaʿa, B002), and ease of the self (B006).
findings.perceptible: The end point is heard as coming back into step with each other. The ground that rose settles again. Turkish 'itaat' (submission to authority) loses the side of mutual agreement.

triggers.how: same surah, same formula: once they withdraw and offer peace, God has given you no way against them
same surah: God will never give disbelievers a way over believers
same surah: God makes a way for women

findings.statement: 'Seek no way against them' plainly forbids further measures once accord returns, and in this surah 'a sabīl over someone' is a recurring figure for a claim or handle against them that is closed the moment hostility ends.
findings.perceptible: The ending uses the same legal and spatial formula the surah uses for a truce in war: when the other party lays down hostility, every road against them is closed. The husband is placed under the same rule. Turkish 'sebil' (a public fountain) loses the road entirely.

triggers.how: same surah: seeking (B001)
concordance: one party transgressing against another
partners wronging one another

findings.statement: Lā tabghū plainly means 'do not seek', and the same verb is the verb of transgression (baghy, B003), so seeking a way against an obedient wife is heard as baghy itself.
findings.perceptible: One word both forbids looking for a pretext and names that pretext as aggression. Turkish 'bağy/bâği' keeps only the rebel. In this ayah the would-be transgressor is the husband.

triggers.how: fixed pair al-ʿAliyy al-Kabīr (22:62, 31:30, 34:23, 40:12)
neighbouring: great sins (B007)

findings.statement: 'High, Great' plainly praises God, and placed here, after the limit on husbands, it reminds anyone tempted to make himself big (takabbur, B006) whose greatness actually counts.
findings.perceptible: The closing attributes work as a warning with a direction. The one who holds power in the household is placed under a greater power. Turkish 'kibir' (arrogance) catches the danger. 'Kebir' as applied to God catches the answer.

triggers.how: plan I6: veering off the road
road image
ḥ-f-ẓ B007: the 'guarding road', straight and never losing its trace

findings.statement: The qawwām plainly stands in charge, and with istiqāma (B008) he stands to keep the household level on the road, while the forbidden 'way against them' is the side-path he may not take.
findings.perceptible: This completes the road image of 4:26–28. Upright standing keeps the course straight. Seeking a sabīl against the wife would be the swerve that appetite-followers want (4:27).

triggers.how: shared lemma: men have a share of what they earned
shared scene body.limbs / posture: standing on the legs

findings.statement: Rijāl plainly means men, and the root is the leg and going on foot (B001, B003), with 'standing on one leg' for earnest effort in a matter (B019).
findings.perceptible: Men are named with a word from the legs they stand on. The next word makes them stand. It is a bodily picture of effort. Turkish 'rical' (notables) adds a prestige the ayah does not give them.

triggers.how: antonym by image: lying down versus standing

findings.statement: Maḍājiʿ are plainly the beds, and the root also means lying slack about one's duty (B003), which stands against the qawwām who must keep standing.
findings.perceptible: There is a quiet contrast between the standing man and the place of lying down. Even the remedy happens in the place of rest. Recorded only.

triggers.how: fitting back together

findings.statement: Nushūz is plainly estrangement, and the same root names God setting bones back in their places and fitting them one onto another (B003, 2:259).
findings.perceptible: The root that names the rising apart also names the re-assembling. This gives a faint prefiguration of 4:35's tawfīq. Recorded only.

loaded_words.role: one who stands persistently for justice and for God, as a witness even against himself
loaded_words.departure: Translations as 'guardians/maintainers' or 'in authority over' make it a rank. The Quranic role is a burdensome duty of upright justice.

loaded_words.role: devotion before God, listed among believers' qualities
loaded_words.departure: 'Obedient (to husbands)' directs toward the husband a word that the Quran otherwise directs toward God.

loaded_words.count: 32 of 49 (plus 9 as the unseen context of belief/fear)
loaded_words.departure: Here it is the circumstance of the husband's absence. The theological role stays audible: her guarding happens where only God sees.

loaded_words.role: a heart-softening reminder, mostly from God, a prophet or a father
loaded_words.count: about 12 of 15 have God, a prophet, Luqman or revelation as the admonisher
loaded_words.departure: 'Advise/lecture' flattens it. The register is the reminding speech of revelation.

loaded_words.role: a route to follow; in 'sabīl ʿalā' a claim or handle against someone
loaded_words.count: 98 of 176 route; 19 of 176 as grounds or means, including 4:34, 4:90, 4:141 in this surah
loaded_words.departure: 'Do not seek means against them' is accurate but loses the surah's formula of a road closed once hostility ends.

loaded_words.departure: 'Do not seek' hides that with ʿalayhinna the verb borders on baghy, aggression.

loaded_words.role: obedience to God and the messenger
loaded_words.departure: Here it is human-to-human, one of only 8 such uses. The root's mutual-accord branch matters.

loaded_words.role: no single role: striking forth an example is dominant

loaded_words.departure: The concordance places 4:34 among the striking uses. The dominant Quranic role of the verb is different, which is why readers hear other senses.

loaded_words.role: divine name, usually paired with kabīr or ʿaẓīm
loaded_words.departure: 'Most High' in a translation cuts the link to the three ʿalā's in the same ayah.

losses.adds: 'Kayyım' adds a court-appointed trustee, and 'yönetici' adds an administrative hierarchy.

losses.loses: The body image of legs and going on foot.
Surplus left after need (B001) and the gift not owed (B003).
losses.adds: 'Fazilet' adds moral superiority, which the ayah does not claim.

losses.loses: Wealth actually leaving and running out, and the everyday household expense in general.
losses.adds: 'Nafaka' adds a court-ordered payment, and 'infak' adds charity.

losses.loses: Reconciliation (ṣulḥ) and being fitting (B002, B003), which link it to iṣlāḥ in 4:35.
losses.adds: Pious and devout in a narrow religious sense.

losses.loses: Long standing and devotion before God.
losses.adds: 'Kunut' adds a specific witr prayer, and 'itaatkâr' adds submissiveness to a person.

losses.loses: Vigilant keeping of honour and pledge, and the husband's absence as a circumstance.
losses.adds: 'Hafız' adds Quran memorisation, and 'gayb' adds the mystical unseen.

losses.loses: Ground rising and jutting, getting up from one's seat, and the fact that either spouse can commit it.
losses.adds: A narrow legal term applied only to wives. 'Serkeşlik' adds an insubordination that belongs to only one side.

losses.loses: A private reminder that softens the heart.
losses.adds: 'Vaaz' adds a pulpit and a public sermon.

losses.loses: Cutting contact within the shared bed as a small departure that can be reversed.
losses.adds: 'Terk' adds abandonment, and 'hicran' adds lasting sorrow.

losses.loses: The Turkish words do not carry the limits the Arabic context sets (the conditional fear, the sequence, the immediate stop).
losses.adds: 'Darp' adds criminal assault and 'dövmek' adds a beating, both heavier than the bounded act the exegetical tradition describes.
Submission to authority in the hierarchical or military sense.

losses.loses: That 'seeking' here borders on aggression (baghy), and the surah's formula of a road against someone being closed.
losses.adds: 'Sebil' adds a public fountain, and 'bağy' adds political rebellion.

losses.loses: The link between ʿAliyy and the three ʿalā's ('over') in the ayah.

grammar: بَعْضَهُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ: the pronoun hum covers men and women together. The ayah does not say 'faḍḍalahum ʿalayhinna' (them over them-feminine), so which party is given more is left as 'some... others'.
بِمَا ... وَبِمَا: two causal clauses ground the qawwāma. The second is a past verb (anfaqū), so the ground is spending that has actually happened.
بِمَا حَفِظَ ٱللَّهُ: mā can be read as 'because / by the fact that God guarded' or as 'by what God guarded (commanded kept)'. Either way God's guarding frames hers.
وَٱلَّٰتِى تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ: the steps are conditioned on fear of nushūz (the anticipation of harm from a sign), not on a proven offence.
فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَٱهْجُرُوهُنَّ ... وَٱضْرِبُوهُنَّ: joined by wa, which does not by itself impose order. The graded sequence is inferred from context by exegetes.
فِى ٱلْمَضَاجِعِ: a locative. The withdrawal happens inside the shared bed.

ٱضْرِبُوهُنَّ: direct object without a preposition, the construction used for striking a person. The restraining, travelling, example and barrier senses of ḍ-r-b each require a different construction.
فَإِنْ أَطَعْنَكُمْ فَلَا تَبْغُوا۟ عَلَيْهِنَّ سَبِيلًا: the fa of the answer closes every measure the moment accord returns. The indefinite sabīlan means 'no way whatsoever'.
variants: حَفِظَ ٱللَّهَ (accusative, listed in the data as mutawātir and attached to 4:34:27): 'by their guarding of God' against the received 'by what God guarded'. Heard together, the two give a keeping in both directions: God guards those who keep God's due in absence.
reread: Men are placed as those who stand, qawwāmūn, like a pillar keeping a household upright. The ground for this is an allotment given 'some over others' and wealth actually spent, and the only other uses of this word in the Quran tie such standing to justice even against oneself. The good wife stands too, but before God (qunūt). She keeps the inside of the house while the husband is away and out of sight, and God keeps watch around her keeping. When the husband sees signs of a rising-up (nushūz), a word also used for the husband himself in 4:128, the remedy has three steps: a reminder in the register God uses with people, a withdrawal kept inside the shared bed, and a strike. The lexicon itself calls a husband's unwarranted strike nushūz, and the ayah stops everything the moment accord returns: in this surah, when hostility ends, no road may be sought against the other party, and seeking one is baghy. The ayah is built on 'over': over women, some over others, no way over them. It ends by naming God al-ʿAliyy, the One who is truly over, and al-Kabīr, so every height in the household stands under His.

set_aside.what: ض ر ب B002 (travelling in the land) as the sense of iḍribūhunna
set_aside.why: This sense requires fī al-arḍ or a similar construction, which is absent here. Kept only as recorded resonance, not as a reading of the verb.

set_aside.what: ض ر ب B003 (striking forth an example), the verb's dominant Quranic role
set_aside.why: It requires mathal as object. The object here is a person.

set_aside.what: ض ر ب B011 (a stallion covering a she-camel) and B016 (trade partnership)
set_aside.why: No trigger in the ayah beyond the root. They would distort the scene.

set_aside.what: ه ج ر B003 (hujr, foul speech) and B004 (a fevered person's raving)
set_aside.why: The plain 'leave' is fixed by 'in the beds'. Foul speech would contradict waʿẓ, the step before.

set_aside.what: ب غ ي B005 (bighāʾ, prostitution) heard in tabghū
set_aside.why: The phonetic overlap with 'seek no way against them' has no trigger and would be offensive noise.
